Missing-Data Treatments for PennDOT Crash Data: MAR vs. MNAR¶

Goal. Starting from two versions of the same 1,000 Pennsylvania crash records, one with values Missing At Random (MAR) and one with values Missing Not At Random (MNAR), we:

  1. profile every variable (histograms plus a data-quality check of what is missing),
  2. check for outliers,
  3. apply three missing-data treatments: mean imputation, median imputation and complete-case removal,
  4. compare original and treated distributions side by side,
  5. fit a logistic regression for FATAL_OR_SUSP_SERIOUS_INJ on every dataset and compare accuracy, F1 and bias.
Variable Meaning Type
SPEEDING At least one vehicle was speeding 0/1
WET_ROAD Wet-road indicator 0/1
YOUNG_DRIVER At least one driver aged 16–20 0/1
HOUR_OF_DAY Hour the crash occurred (0–23) integer
PERSON_COUNT Total people involved count
FATAL_OR_SUSP_SERIOUS_INJ (target) At least one person killed or suspected serious injury 0/1

How to read the colors throughout: ■ Original (untreated) · ■ Mean imputation · ■ Median imputation · ■ Complete case · ■ Reference (best-available truth)

1. Load the data¶

The two files use slightly different column names (HOUR in MAR vs. HOUR_OF_DAY in MNAR, plus Person count), so we harmonize them first. Also note: the worksheet inside MNAR_ex1.xls is named MCAR_ex1. The file name and the assignment both say MNAR, and the missingness pattern below confirms it is not completely at random.

In [2]:
def load(path):
    df = pd.read_excel(DATA_DIR / path)
    df = df.rename(columns={"HOUR": "HOUR_OF_DAY", "Person count": "PERSON_COUNT"})
    return df[COLS]

raw = {"MAR": load("MAR_ex1.xls"), "MNAR": load("MNAR_ex1.xls")}
for m, df in raw.items():

1a. Building a reference ("best-available truth") dataset¶

To say which treatment is less biased, we need the real values that are hidden behind the gaps. We can get them because of how the files relate:

  • MAR_ex1.xls, MNAR_ex1.xls and the first 1,000 rows of the full extract features.xls are the same 1,000 crashes in the same row order.
  • MAR and MNAR hide different cells, and features.xls has its own, different gaps. A value that is missing in one file is often present in another.

We build the reference in two steps. The source files are never modified; everything happens in memory in a new table called reference.

Step 1 — Combine the three files. For each cell, take the value from whichever file has it. This is only valid if the files never contradict each other, which is checked first.

In [3]:
features_full = pd.read_excel(DATA_DIR / "features.xls").dropna(how="all").reset_index(drop=True).iloc[:1000]
features = features_full[COLS]

# Validity check: wherever two files both have a value, it must be the same value
for a_name, b_name, a, b in [("MAR", "MNAR", raw["MAR"], raw["MNAR"]),
                             ("MAR", "features", raw["MAR"], features),
                             ("MNAR", "features", raw["MNAR"], features)]:
    both = a.notna() & b.notna()
    print(f"{a_name:>4} vs {b_name:<8}: {int(((a != b) & both).sum().sum())} disagreeing cells "
          f"out of {int(both.sum().sum()):,} cells observed in both")

recon = raw["MAR"].fillna(raw["MNAR"]).fillna(features)
print("\nCells still unknown after combining the 3 files:", recon.isna().sum()[lambda s: s > 0].to_dict())

 MAR vs MNAR    : 0 disagreeing cells out of 5,172 cells observed in both
 MAR vs features: 0 disagreeing cells out of 5,547 cells observed in both
MNAR vs features: 0 disagreeing cells out of 5,172 cells observed in both

Cells still unknown after combining the 3 files: {'WET_ROAD': 44, 'YOUNG_DRIVER': 49}

The files agree on every shared cell, so combining them is safe. That recovers every value except 44 WET_ROAD and 49 YOUNG_DRIVER cells, which are blank in all three files.

Step 2: derive the last 93 cells from related source fields. features.xls contains the fields these flags are based on, and those fields have no gaps. Using the PennDOT Crash Data Dictionary (Crash_Data_Dictionary_2026.pdf):

Flag Dictionary definition Source field(s) Derivation rule
WET_ROAD "Wet Road Indicator" (0 = No, 1 = Yes) ROAD_CONDITION (roadway surface condition code) 1 if ROAD_CONDITION is 08 or 09, else 0
YOUNG_DRIVER "The crash involved at least 1 driver age 16–20" DRIVER_COUNT_16YR … DRIVER_COUNT_20YR ("total number of N-year-old drivers") 1 if any of the five counts > 0, else 0

ROAD_CONDITION codes from the dictionary: 01 Dry · 02 Ice/Frost · 03 Mud, Dirt, Gravel · 04 Oil · 05 Sand · 06 Slush · 07 Snow · 08 Water (Standing or Moving) · 09 Wet · 22 Mud, Sand, Dirt, Oil (expired) · 98 Other · 99 Unknown.

How each rule is justified

  • YOUNG_DRIVER follows directly from the dictionary: "at least one driver aged 16–20" is the same as "the count of drivers aged 16–20 is above zero".
  • WET_ROAD: the dictionary does not list which codes set the flag, so the rule was learned from the data. In every crash where both are known, WET_ROAD = 1 for codes 08 and 09 and WET_ROAD = 0 for every other code (table below). Snow (07), slush (06) and ice (02) are not counted as wet.

The tables below test each rule against every cell where the true flag is known.

In [4]:
WET_CODES = [8, 9]   # 08 = Water (standing or moving), 09 = Wet
YOUNG_COUNT_COLS = [f"DRIVER_COUNT_{age}YR" for age in range(16, 21)]
ROAD_LABELS = {1: "01 Dry", 2: "02 Ice/Frost", 3: "03 Mud, Dirt, Gravel", 4: "04 Oil", 5: "05 Sand", 6: "06 Slush",
               7: "07 Snow", 8: "08 Water", 9: "09 Wet", 22: "22 Mud/Sand/Dirt/Oil", 98: "98 Other", 99: "99 Unknown"}

derived = pd.DataFrame({
    "WET_ROAD": features_full["ROAD_CONDITION"].isin(WET_CODES).astype(float),
    "YOUNG_DRIVER": (features_full[YOUNG_COUNT_COLS].sum(axis=1) > 0).astype(float)})

# Evidence 1: recorded WET_ROAD flag by road-surface code (known cells only)
known = recon["WET_ROAD"].notna()
wet_check = pd.crosstab(features_full.loc[known, "ROAD_CONDITION"].map(ROAD_LABELS),
                        recon.loc[known, "WET_ROAD"].map({0: "WET_ROAD = 0", 1: "WET_ROAD = 1"}))
wet_check["Rule gives"] = [int(int(lbl[:2]) in WET_CODES) for lbl in wet_check.index]
display(wet_check.style.set_caption("Recorded WET_ROAD flag by ROAD_CONDITION code (cells where the flag is known)"))

# Evidence 2: recorded YOUNG_DRIVER flag vs. "any driver aged 16-20" (known cells only)
known = recon["YOUNG_DRIVER"].notna()
yd_check = pd.crosstab(derived.loc[known, "YOUNG_DRIVER"].map({0: "Rule: no driver 16-20", 1: "Rule: driver 16-20 present"}),
                       recon.loc[known, "YOUNG_DRIVER"].map({0: "YOUNG_DRIVER = 0", 1: "YOUNG_DRIVER = 1"}))
display(yd_check.style.set_caption("Recorded YOUNG_DRIVER flag vs. the driver-age-count rule (cells where the flag is known)"))

rows = []
for c in derived:
    known = recon[c].notna(); gap = recon[c].isna()
    rows.append({"Flag": c, "Known cells tested": int(known.sum()),
                 "Rule agrees": int((derived.loc[known, c] == recon.loc[known, c]).sum()),
                 "Agreement": (derived.loc[known, c] == recon.loc[known, c]).mean(),
                 "Cells filled by rule": int(gap.sum()), "…filled as 1": int(derived.loc[gap, c].sum())})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Flag").style.format({"Agreement": "{:.1%}"}).set_caption("Rule validation summary"))

conflicts = recon["YOUNG_DRIVER"].notna() & (derived["YOUNG_DRIVER"] != recon["YOUNG_DRIVER"])
print("Rows where YOUNG_DRIVER = 1 but all five 16–20 driver counts are 0:", conflicts[conflicts].index.tolist())

recon[["WET_ROAD", "YOUNG_DRIVER"]] = recon[["WET_ROAD", "YOUNG_DRIVER"]].fillna(derived)
reference = recon.astype(float)
assert reference.notna().all().all()
print(f"\nReference dataset: {len(reference):,} complete rows, 0 missing cells")

TRUE_FATAL = reference[TARGET].mean()
ref_means = reference[COLS].mean()

What the validation shows

  • WET_ROAD rule: 100% agreement with all 956 known flags. Every crash coded 08 or 09 is flagged wet, and every other code is not. The 44 cells it fills have codes 01 (Dry, 35 cells → 0) and 09 (Wet, 9 cells → 1), which are the two most common, unambiguous codes.
  • YOUNG_DRIVER rule: 99.7% agreement (948 of 951). The only conflicts are 3 rows where the flag says 1 but every 16–20 driver count is 0. That is an inconsistency inside the source data, not a fault in the rule. The reverse never happens: no row has a 16–20 driver count above zero but a flag of 0. Of the 49 cells the rule fills, 9 become 1 and 40 become 0. At most a fraction of one of those 40 zeros is expected to be wrong.

Result: a complete 1,000-row reference. About 99% of its cells are recorded values, and the remaining 93 are derived by rules validated above. It is not guaranteed perfect ground truth, so this notebook calls it the "best-available truth", but it is accurate enough to measure bias against. Every later use of "bias" (the black ◆ in the histograms, the colored means table, the "tested on true values" evaluation and the coefficient comparison) means distance from this reference.

2. Data-quality check: what is missing?¶

def missing_table(df):
    return pd.DataFrame({"Missing (n)": df.isna().sum(), "Missing (%)": df.isna().mean() * 100})

mt = pd.concat({m: missing_table(raw[m]) for m in MECHS}, axis=1)
summary_row = pd.DataFrame({(m, c): [v] for m in MECHS for c, v in
                            [("Missing (n)", raw[m].isna().any(axis=1).sum()),
                             ("Missing (%)", raw[m].isna().any(axis=1).mean() * 100)]},
                           index=["ANY column (rows affected)"])
mt = pd.concat([mt, summary_row])
(mt.style.format({c: "{:.0f}" if c[1] == "Missing (n)" else "{:.1f}%" for c in mt.columns})
   .background_gradient(cmap="Blues", subset=[c for c in mt.columns if c[1] == "Missing (%)"], vmin=0, vmax=40)
   .set_caption("Missing values per column"))

Direct MNAR check: are the hidden values different from the observed ones?¶

MNAR means that whether a value is missing depends on the hidden value itself. Normally that can't be tested, because the hidden values are unknown. Here the reference (section 1a) shows us what was hidden, so we can test it directly with two checks:

  • Raw gap: compare the true values in hidden cells with the values in observed cells. The p-value comes from Fisher's exact test for the 0/1 flags and a Mann–Whitney test for PERSON_COUNT.
  • Conditional test: a logistic regression of is this cell missing? on the cell's true value, controlling for the always-observed variables (SPEEDING, HOUR_OF_DAY and the target). Under MAR, missingness can depend on observed variables but not on the hidden value, so the true value should have no effect once those are controlled for. A significant effect points to MNAR.
In [8]:
from scipy.stats import fisher_exact, mannwhitneyu

ALWAYS_OBSERVED = ["SPEEDING", "HOUR_OF_DAY", TARGET]
rows = []
for m in MECHS:
    for c in ["WET_ROAD", "YOUNG_DRIVER", "PERSON_COUNT"]:
        miss = raw[m][c].isna()
        tv = reference[c]
        if c in BINARY:
            h, o = int(tv[miss].sum()), int(tv[~miss].sum())
            p_raw = fisher_exact([[h, miss.sum() - h], [o, (~miss).sum() - o]])[1]
        else:
            p_raw = mannwhitneyu(tv[miss], tv[~miss])[1]
        X = sm.add_constant(pd.concat([tv, raw[m][ALWAYS_OBSERVED]], axis=1).astype(float))
        p_cond = sm.Logit(miss.astype(float), X).fit(disp=0).pvalues[c]
        rows.append({"Dataset": m, "Variable": c, "Hidden cells": int(miss.sum()),
                     "True mean where HIDDEN": tv[miss].mean(), "Mean where OBSERVED": tv[~miss].mean(),
                     "p (raw gap)": p_raw, "p (controlling for observed vars)": p_cond})
hid = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["Dataset", "Variable"])
hid.insert(3, "Gap (hidden − observed)", hid["True mean where HIDDEN"] - hid["Mean where OBSERVED"])

def shade_p(v):
    return ("background-color: #f4c7c3; font-weight: bold" if v < 0.05 else
            "background-color: #fbe5d6" if v < 0.10 else "")

(hid.style.format({"True mean where HIDDEN": "{:.3f}", "Mean where OBSERVED": "{:.3f}",
                   "Gap (hidden − observed)": "{:+.3f}", "p (raw gap)": "{:.3f}",
                   "p (controlling for observed vars)": "{:.3f}"})
    .background_gradient(cmap="RdBu_r", subset=["Gap (hidden − observed)"], vmin=-0.06, vmax=0.06)
    .map(shade_p, subset=["p (raw gap)", "p (controlling for observed vars)"])
    .set_caption("Hidden vs. observed values (p-value shading: red = below 0.05, light = below 0.10)"))

MNAR WET_ROAD 234 0.184 0.133 +0.051 0.057 0.051

PERSON_COUNT 69 2.681 2.344 +0.337 0.062 0.293

How to read this: under MAR, both p-values should be large. Under MNAR, the conditional p-value should be small for at least one variable.

  • MAR: the hidden values look like the observed ones, and the hidden value does not predict missingness (every conditional p-value is 0.29 or higher). This is consistent with MAR.
  • MNAR: wet roads were about 40% more common among hidden cells (18.4% vs. 13.3%), and that effect holds after controlling for the observed variables (p ≈ 0.05). YOUNG_DRIVER points the expected direction (hidden rows had fewer young drivers) but is not significant (p ≈ 0.17).
  • PERSON_COUNT (identical in both files): the hidden crashes involved more people (raw p ≈ 0.06), but the effect largely disappears once observed variables are controlled for (p ≈ 0.29). That looks more like MAR than MNAR.

Bottom line: this check supports the MNAR label for the MNAR file, mainly through WET_ROAD, but the evidence is borderline, not conclusive. With 1,000 rows and rare outcomes, the signal sits at the edge of statistical significance.

Data-quality findings

  • SPEEDING, HOUR_OF_DAY and the target are complete in both files. Missingness hits only WET_ROAD, YOUNG_DRIVER and PERSON_COUNT.
  • PERSON_COUNT is missing in exactly the same 69 rows (6.9%) in both files, so this part of the problem is identical across the two datasets.
  • MAR: WET_ROAD (18.4%) and YOUNG_DRIVER (20.0%) are missing mostly in different rows, so 38.5% of rows have at least one gap. The hidden true values are close to the observed ones (wet roads 15.2% hidden vs. 14.3% observed). However, rows with WET_ROAD missing have a higher fatal rate (7.6% vs. 4.5%, p ≈ 0.10). That is allowed under MAR, because missingness may depend on a variable we do observe (here, the target). It still means that dropping those rows will remove fatal crashes.
  • MNAR: WET_ROAD and YOUNG_DRIVER are missing together in the same 234 rows (23.4%). The hidden rows contain more wet roads (18.4% vs. 13.3%) and fewer young drivers (14.5% vs. 18.5%) than the observed rows, and they have a higher fatal/serious-injury rate (7.3% vs. 4.4%, p ≈ 0.09). This is the MNAR pattern: whether a value gets recorded depends on the value itself. The evidence is clearest for WET_ROAD (p ≈ 0.05 after controlling for observed variables) and weaker for YOUNG_DRIVER. To the extent this holds, the observed data is a biased sample, and no treatment that only uses the observed values can correct for it.
  • The PERSON_COUNT gaps are not completely random either. Crashes with a missing person count actually involved more people (true mean 2.68 vs. 2.34 observed). This is mostly explained by observed variables, though, so it behaves more like MAR.
  • Duplicates: with only 6 low-cardinality columns, many rows are identical by design (531 duplicated 6-column rows), which is not an error. In the 80-column features.xls, however, 25 rows are exact duplicates, and some crashes appear 2–3 times (e.g. rows 160–162, rows 524–525) with only SPEED_LIMIT differing. These look like one crash repeated per road segment or unit. It is worth confirming with the data owner, since repeated rows inflate the effective sample size.

3. Outlier check¶

The binary variables can only be 0/1 (verified below), so outliers can only occur in HOUR_OF_DAY and PERSON_COUNT.

In [9]:
df0 = raw["MAR"]
for c in BINARY:
    assert set(df0[c].dropna().unique()) <= {0, 1}, c
print("All binary columns contain only 0/1 ✓;  HOUR_OF_DAY range:", df0.HOUR_OF_DAY.min(), "–", df0.HOUR_OF_DAY.max())

def iqr_outliers(s):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    z = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
    return pd.Series({"Q1": q1, "Q3": q3, "Lower fence": lo, "Upper fence": hi,
                      "# below": int((s < lo).sum()), "# above": int((s > hi).sum()),
                      "# |z| > 3": int((z.abs() > 3).sum()), "Max": s.max()})

pd.DataFrame({c: iqr_outliers(df0[c].dropna()) for c in ["HOUR_OF_DAY", "PERSON_COUNT"]}).T

Outlier findings

  • PERSON_COUNT = 48 (rows 524–525). This is a genuine extreme: features.xls shows the crash involved a school bus. It is not a data-entry error, so we keep it. It does pull the mean upward (mean ≈ 2.34 vs. median 2), which matters for mean imputation.
  • PERSON_COUNT of 7–9 are flagged by the IQR rule (fence = 6), but they are plausible multi-occupant crashes. We keep them.
  • PERSON_COUNT = 0 (4 rows: 160–162, 316) is suspicious. Every reportable crash involves at least one driver. These are probably hit-and-run or unknown-occupant records, and they are also among the duplicated rows noted above. We flag them and keep them so that every treatment starts from the same data.
  • HOUR_OF_DAY: all values fall in 0–23 and there are no outliers. (Treating hour as a linear number ignores that 23:00 and 00:00 are adjacent. We keep it numeric because the assignment defines it that way.)
  • SPEEDING is rare (3.2%) but that is a real class imbalance, not an outlier.

4. Apply the missing-data treatments¶

For each mechanism we create three new datasets:

Treatment What it does Side effect to watch for
Mean Replace each missing value with the column mean Binary columns get fractional values (e.g. 0.14), and variance shrinks
Median Replace each missing value with the column median Binary columns: the median is 0, so every gap becomes "No"
Complete case Drop any row with a missing value Loses rows; biased when missingness depends on the values (MNAR)

All 8 datasets (original plus three treatments, for each mechanism) are also saved as CSV in treated_datasets/.

In [11]:
def treat(df, how):
    if how == "Original":      return df.copy()
    if how == "Mean":          return df.fillna(df.mean())
    if how == "Median":        return df.fillna(df.median())
    if how == "Complete case": return df.dropna().reset_index(drop=True)

datasets = {(m, t): treat(raw[m], t) for m in MECHS for t in TREATMENTS}

    d.to_csv(OUT_DIR / f"{m}_{t.lower().replace(' ', '_')}.csv", index=False)

5. Side-by-side histograms: original vs. treated¶

Each figure covers one mechanism. Rows are variables, columns are datasets. The y-axis is the share of rows, so a column with fewer rows (complete case) stays comparable, and every row of panels shares one y-scale. For the 0/1 and count variables, each distinct value gets its own bar:

  • gray “Missing” bar: the share of rows with no value (original data only),
  • hatched bar marked *: a value created by imputation that does not exist in the real data (e.g. 0.14* = 14% of a "yes"),
  • black ◆: the reference (best-available truth) share for that value, so you can see which treatment lands closest.
In [12]:
def _key(v, cap):
    if pd.isna(v): return "Missing"
    if cap is not None and v > cap: return f">{cap}"
    return str(int(v)) if float(v).is_integer() else f"{v:.2f}*"

def _order(k):
    if k == "Missing": return (3, 0)
    if k.startswith(">"): return (2, 0)
    return (1, float(k.rstrip("*")))

def shares(s, cap=None):
    out = s.map(lambda v: _key(v, cap)).value_counts(normalize=True)
    return out

def hist_grid(mech, cap=10):
    cols = [(t, datasets[(mech, t)]) for t in TREATMENTS]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(COLS), len(cols), figsize=(17, 3.0 * len(COLS)), sharey="row")
    for r, var in enumerate([TARGET] + PREDICTORS):
        if var == "HOUR_OF_DAY":
            ref = reference[var].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index()
            for c, (t, d) in enumerate(cols):
                ax = axes[r, c]
                ax.hist(d[var].dropna(), bins=np.arange(-0.5, 24.5), weights=np.full(d[var].notna().sum(), 1 / len(d)),
                        color=COLORS[t], edgecolor="white", linewidth=1)
                ax.plot(ref.index, ref.values, color=COLORS["Reference"], lw=1.2, marker="D", ms=2.5, label="Reference")
                ax.set_xticks(range(0, 24, 3))
        else:
            k = None if var in BINARY else cap
            sh = {t: shares(d[var], k) for t, d in cols}
            ref = shares(reference[var], k)
            cats = sorted(set().union(*[s.index for s in sh.values()], ref.index), key=_order)
            for c, (t, d) in enumerate(cols):
                ax = axes[r, c]
                vals = sh[t].reindex(cats, fill_value=0)
                for i, (cat, v) in enumerate(vals.items()):
                    is_missing, is_imputed = cat == "Missing", cat.endswith("*")
                    ax.bar(i, v, width=0.8, color=MISSING_COLOR if is_missing else COLORS[t],
                           hatch="///" if is_imputed else None, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.5)
                    if v > 0 and (var in BINARY or v >= 0.04):
                        ax.text(i, v, f"{v:.1%}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5, color="#52514e")
                rv = ref.reindex(cats)
                ax.scatter(range(len(cats)), rv.values, marker="D", s=22, color=COLORS["Reference"], zorder=5,
                           edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, label="Reference")
                ax.set_xticks(range(len(cats)), cats, fontsize=8)
        for c, (t, d) in enumerate(cols):
            ax = axes[r, c]
            ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))
            ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
            if r == 0:
                ax.set_title(f"{t}\n(n = {len(d):,})", fontsize=12, color=COLORS[t] if t != "Original" else "#52514e")
        axes[r, 0].set_ylabel(var.replace("_", " ").replace("FATAL OR SUSP SERIOUS INJ", "FATAL/SERIOUS INJ\n(target)"),
                              fontsize=9.5, fontweight="semibold")
    axes[0, -1].legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle(f"{mech} dataset: distribution of every variable, original vs. each treatment", fontsize=15, y=1.0)
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

5a. The same comparison as one table: how far does each dataset sit from the truth?¶

Each cell shows the variable's mean (for a 0/1 variable, the share of "yes"). The color shows the difference from the reference: red = too high, blue = too low, white = unbiased. For the original data, means are computed over the observed values only.

In [15]:
rows = []
for (m, t), d in datasets.items():
    rows.append({"Dataset": m, "Treatment": t, **d[COLS].mean().to_dict()})
means = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["Dataset", "Treatment"])
means.loc[("Reference", "best-available truth"), :] = ref_means
delta = means - ref_means

def color_by_delta(_):
    styles = pd.DataFrame("", index=means.index, columns=means.columns)
    for c in means.columns:
        scale = max(abs(delta[c]).max(), 1e-9)
        for i in means.index:
            x = delta.loc[i, c] / scale
            rgb = plt.cm.RdBu_r(0.5 + 0.45 * x)
            styles.loc[i, c] = f"background-color: rgba({int(rgb[0]*255)},{int(rgb[1]*255)},{int(rgb[2]*255)},0.85)"
    return styles

      .format("{:.3f}").format("{:.2f}", subset=["HOUR_OF_DAY", "PERSON_COUNT"])
      .set_caption("Variable means by dataset (color = bias vs. reference)"))

6. Logistic regression on every dataset¶

Setup

  • Model: FATAL_OR_SUSP_SERIOUS_INJ ~ SPEEDING + WET_ROAD + YOUNG_DRIVER + HOUR_OF_DAY + PERSON_COUNT, with standardized inputs.
  • Class imbalance: only 5.1% of crashes are fatal/serious. An ordinary logistic regression simply predicts "no" every time. That scores ~95% accuracy but an F1 of 0 (demonstrated below). We therefore use class_weight="balanced", which makes the model actually try to find the fatal crashes. Accuracy then falls below 95%, and that is expected.
  • Evaluation: stratified 5-fold cross-validation repeated 20 times (100 fits per dataset). We report the mean ± standard deviation, because with only ~50 positive cases a single train/test split would be very noisy.
  • The "Original" datasets cannot be passed to a logistic regression with gaps in them. Standard software (R glm, statsmodels) silently drops incomplete rows, so modeling the original data is complete-case analysis. The original is therefore represented by the complete-case model, and we add the Reference model as the benchmark.
In [17]:
CV = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=20, random_state=42)
SCORING = {"Accuracy": "accuracy", "F1": "f1", "Recall": "recall", "Precision": "precision", "ROC AUC": "roc_auc"}
MODEL_SETS = [(m, t) for m in MECHS for t in ["Mean", "Median", "Complete case"]]

def model(weighted=True):
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced" if weighted else None, max_iter=2000))

# Why class weighting is necessary

r = cross_validate(model(weighted=False), d[PREDICTORS], d[TARGET], cv=CV, scoring=SCORING)

      f"accuracy = {r['test_Accuracy'].mean():.3f},  F1 = {r['test_F1'].mean():.3f},  recall = {r['test_Recall'].mean():.3f}"
      "\n→ it predicts 'not fatal' for everyone, so we use class_weight='balanced' from here on.")

6a. A fair head-to-head: train on the treated data, test on the true data¶

The table above scores each model on its own (treated) data. Complete-case models are tested only on "easy" complete rows, and imputed models are tested against imputed values. To compare like with like, we also run a second evaluation. The same 1,000 rows are split into the same folds for every treatment. Each model is trained on its treated training rows (imputation statistics are computed from the training rows only, so nothing leaks), and every model is then tested on the same held-out rows using their true reference values. This measures what we actually care about: how well a model built on each treatment performs in the real world.

In [20]:
y_all = reference[TARGET].values
cv_fair = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=20, random_state=7)

fair = []
for m in MECHS:
    for t in ["Mean", "Median", "Complete case", "Reference"]:
        scores = {k: [] for k in ["Accuracy", "F1", "ROC AUC", "Recall"]}
        for tr, te in cv_fair.split(np.zeros(1000), y_all):
            train = reference.iloc[tr] if t == "Reference" else treat(raw[m].iloc[tr], t)
            test = reference.iloc[te]
            clf = model().fit(train[PREDICTORS], train[TARGET])
            p = clf.predict(test[PREDICTORS]); pr = clf.predict_proba(test[PREDICTORS])[:, 1]
            scores["Accuracy"].append(accuracy_score(test[TARGET], p))
            scores["F1"].append(f1_score(test[TARGET], p))
            scores["Recall"].append(recall_score(test[TARGET], p))
            scores["ROC AUC"].append(roc_auc_score(test[TARGET], pr))
        fair.append({"Dataset": m, "Treatment": t, **{k: np.mean(v) for k, v in scores.items()},
                     **{f"{k} sd": np.std(v) for k, v in scores.items()}})
fair = pd.DataFrame(fair)
fair_show = fair.pivot(index="Treatment", columns="Dataset", values=["Accuracy", "F1", "ROC AUC"]).reindex(["Mean", "Median", "Complete case", "Reference"])

   .set_caption("Tested on TRUE values of the same held-out rows (higher = better)"))

      % (fair["F1 sd"].mean(), fair["Accuracy sd"].mean(), fair["ROC AUC sd"].mean()))

7. Which missing-data method is less biased?¶

Accuracy and F1 tell us how well a model predicts. Bias asks whether the model learned the right relationship. To measure it, we fit an unpenalized logistic regression (statsmodels) on each dataset with the raw, unscaled predictors, and compare its odds ratios with the odds ratios from the reference data.

In [21]:
def fit_logit(d):
    X = sm.add_constant(d[PREDICTORS].astype(float))
    res = sm.Logit(d[TARGET].astype(float), X).fit(disp=0, maxiter=200)
    ci = res.conf_int()
    return pd.DataFrame({"coef": res.params, "lo": ci[0], "hi": ci[1], "p": res.pvalues}).drop("const")

coefs = {(m, t): fit_logit(model_data[(m, t)]) for (m, t) in model_data}
ref_coef = coefs[("Reference", "Reference")]

or_tbl = pd.DataFrame({f"{m} · {t}" if m != "Reference" else "Reference": np.exp(c["coef"]) for (m, t), c in coefs.items()}).T
or_tbl.index.name = "Odds ratio for…"
(or_tbl.style.format("{:.2f}")
   .apply(lambda col: ["font-weight: bold; border-top: 2px solid #0b0b0b" if i == "Reference" else "" for i in col.index])
   .background_gradient(cmap="PuOr_r", axis=None, vmin=0.3, vmax=3.0)
   .set_caption("Odds ratios (per 1-unit change): how much each factor multiplies the odds of a fatal/serious crash"))

    r0 = ref_coef.loc[var]
    ax.axvspan(np.exp(r0.lo), np.exp(r0.hi), color="#d6d5d0", alpha=0.45, lw=0)
    ax.axvline(np.exp(r0.coef), color=COLORS["Reference"], lw=1.6)
    ax.axvline(1, color="#8a8986", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    for i, (m, t) in enumerate(order):
        c = coefs[(m, t)].loc[var]
        y = i + (0.5 if m == "MNAR" else 0)
        ax.plot([np.exp(c.lo), np.exp(c.hi)], [y, y], color=COLORS[t], lw=2, solid_capstyle="round")
        ax.scatter(np.exp(c.coef), y, s=60, color=COLORS[t], edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
    if var in BINARY:
        ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("Odds ratio (log scale)")
        ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:g}"))
        ax.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(mtick.NullFormatter())
    else:
        ax.set_xlabel("Odds ratio per +1 unit")
    ax.set_title(var)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
axes[0].set_yticks([i + (0.5 if m == "MNAR" else 0) for i, (m, _) in enumerate(order)], ylabels)
axes[0].invert_yaxis()
axes[0].axhline(2.75, color="#b5b4ae", lw=0.8)
fig.suptitle("Odds ratios by treatment. Black line = reference; gray band = reference 95% CI; dotted = no effect",
             fontsize=13, y=1.03)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Bias scorecard: lower = closer to the truth
ref_sd = reference[PREDICTORS].std()
rows = []
for (m, t) in order:
    c = coefs[(m, t)]
    d = model_data[(m, t)]
    coef_err = (c["coef"] - ref_coef["coef"]) * ref_sd   # per-SD scale so all 5 predictors are comparable
    rows.append({"Dataset": m, "Treatment": t,
                 "Rows used": len(d),
                 "|Δ fatal rate| (pts)": abs(d[TARGET].mean() - TRUE_FATAL) * 100,
                 "|Δ WET_ROAD mean| (pts)": abs(d.WET_ROAD.mean() - ref_means.WET_ROAD) * 100,
                 "|Δ YOUNG_DRIVER mean| (pts)": abs(d.YOUNG_DRIVER.mean() - ref_means.YOUNG_DRIVER) * 100,
                 "|Δ PERSON_COUNT mean|": abs(d.PERSON_COUNT.mean() - ref_means.PERSON_COUNT),
                 "|Δ coef| SPEEDING": abs(coef_err["SPEEDING"]),
                 "|Δ coef| WET_ROAD": abs(coef_err["WET_ROAD"]),
                 "|Δ coef| YOUNG_DRIVER": abs(coef_err["YOUNG_DRIVER"]),
                 "|Δ coef| PERSON_COUNT": abs(coef_err["PERSON_COUNT"]),
                 "Coef RMSE (per-SD)": np.sqrt((coef_err ** 2).mean()),
                 "SE inflation vs ref": ((c.hi - c.lo) / (ref_coef.hi - ref_coef.lo)).mean()})
score = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index(["Dataset", "Treatment"])
score["Rank (by coef RMSE, within dataset)"] = score.groupby(level=0)["Coef RMSE (per-SD)"].rank().astype(int)
score.columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
    [("", c) if c == "Rows used" else ("Distribution bias", c) if "mean" in c or "rate" in c else ("Model (coefficient) bias", c)
     for c in score.columns])
(score.style.format("{:.3f}").format("{:.0f}", subset=[c for c in score.columns if c[1] in ("Rows used", "Rank (by coef RMSE, within dataset)")])
      .format("{:.2f}×", subset=[c for c in score.columns if c[1] == "SE inflation vs ref"])
      .background_gradient(cmap="Reds", subset=[c for c in score.columns if c[1].startswith("|") or "RMSE" in c[1]], axis=0)
      .set_caption("Bias scorecard vs. reference (Δ = distance from reference; lower / lighter = less biased)"))

8. Final summary¶

What the data looked like¶

  • Two clean predictors and the target were complete: SPEEDING, HOUR_OF_DAY and FATAL_OR_SUSP_SERIOUS_INJ (5.1% positive, 51 of 1,000 crashes). Missingness affects only WET_ROAD, YOUNG_DRIVER and PERSON_COUNT.
  • Outliers: PERSON_COUNT = 48 is real (a school-bus crash), so we kept it. Four crashes with PERSON_COUNT = 0 are implausible and should be reviewed. HOUR_OF_DAY has no outliers. A few crash records appear to be duplicated in the source extract.
  • Because the MAR and MNAR files are the same 1,000 crashes, we could rebuild a complete reference (best-available truth) and measure bias directly instead of guessing at it.

Treatment by treatment¶

MAR (missing at random) MNAR (missing not at random)
Mean imputation Keeps every variable's mean almost exactly right (within 0.4 pts). It does create fake “0.14 / 0.18” values in yes/no fields and squashes variance. Least distribution bias. It can only reproduce the observed mean, and that mean is already wrong: wet roads are under-counted by ~1.2 pts (−8%) and young drivers over-counted by ~0.9 pts. It ties for least model bias.
Median imputation For a 0/1 variable the median is 0, so every gap becomes “no”. This understates wet roads by 2.8 pts (−19%) and young drivers by 3.2 pts (−18%). Its model coefficients happened to land closest to the reference, but the margin is small. The worst distortion of the predictors of any treatment: wet roads −4.3 pts (−30%), young drivers −3.4 pts (−19%). Model bias is about the same as mean imputation.
Complete-case removal Throws away 38.5% of rows and 45% of the fatal crashes (51 → 28). The fatal rate falls to 4.6%. Confidence intervals are ~40% wider and the coefficients are the most biased. Throws away 29% of rows, and the fatal rate falls to 4.4% (−14%) because the dropped rows were disproportionately severe. Coefficients are ~2× more biased than with imputation (e.g. speeding's odds ratio is 7.5 vs. 4.0 in the reference) and intervals are ~64% wider. The most biased option overall.

Model performance (accuracy & F1)¶

  • Accuracy is misleading here. A model that never predicts a fatal crash scores 94.9% accuracy with an F1 of 0. With class-balanced weights, accuracy falls to ~0.57–0.65 and F1 rises to ~0.08–0.10.
  • All the models are weak. ROC AUC is only 0.51–0.58, barely above chance. Of the five predictors, only SPEEDING has a statistically significant effect (odds ratio ≈ 4, p ≈ 0.007). The remaining four contribute little signal.
  • The differences between treatments are smaller than the noise. When every model is tested on the same held-out rows using true values, F1 ranges from 0.085 to 0.099 and accuracy from 0.58 to 0.64. The fold-to-fold standard deviation is ~0.034 for F1 and ~0.07 for accuracy. No treatment gives a meaningfully better predictive model.
  • The MNAR complete-case model looks best when scored on its own data (accuracy 0.646, F1 0.102, AUC 0.581). That is an illusion: it is evaluated only on the rows that survived the MNAR filter, which are an easier, less severe subset.

Which method is less biased?¶

  1. Complete-case removal is the most biased under both mechanisms, and the problem is much worse under MNAR. Under MNAR the dropped rows differ systematically (more wet roads, more severe crashes), so deleting them shifts the fatal rate, inflates the speeding effect and widens every confidence interval. Even under MAR it lost 45% of the already rare fatal cases.
  2. Mean imputation is the least biased simple method overall. It preserves the variable averages (exactly so under MAR) and keeps the model coefficients close to the reference.
  3. Median imputation should be avoided for binary variables. It silently recodes every missing value as "no", which is a large distortion of the predictor distributions under both mechanisms. On model coefficients it performed about as well as mean imputation.
  4. MAR vs. MNAR: under MAR, the simple imputations come close to the truth. Under MNAR, every method stays biased. A treatment that only uses the observed values cannot know that the hidden roads were wetter, so mean imputation inherits the observed-data bias and median imputation adds more on top.

Recommendations¶

  • Recover the values from the source instead of imputing them. WET_ROAD can be derived from ROAD_CONDITION (codes 08 Water and 09 Wet; 100% agreement with known flags) and YOUNG_DRIVER from the 16–20 driver-age counts (99.7% agreement) in features.xls (section 1a). That removes the missing-data problem entirely.
  • If recovery is not possible: use multiple imputation (e.g. MICE) with auxiliary variables plus a missingness-indicator column, and run a sensitivity analysis for the MNAR case.
  • Report F1, recall and ROC AUC rather than accuracy for this imbalanced outcome, and add stronger predictors (e.g. unbelted occupants, impairment, speed limit, pedestrian involvement) before relying on the model.
